html:
Surah Al-Ikhlāṣ (The Sincere Creed, lit. Sincerity or Purifying) is the 112th surah of the Qur’an — four short verses, Makkī by the dominant classification of Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī, with a minority Madanī opinion that links it to an occasion of revelation in Madinah when Jewish or Christian interlocutors asked the Prophet ﷺ to describe his Lord. The surah forms the third of al-Mu‘awwidhāt — the trio recited together with Al-Falaq and An-Nās — but unlike its two pair-mates it is not a refuge formula. Al-Ikhlāṣ is pure ʿaqīdah: a four-verse creed that distills the entire doctrine of tawḥīd into a declaration a child can memorise and a philosopher cannot exhaust. Ibn Taymiyyah in Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā frames the surah structurally against the two Mu‘awwidhatān: Al-Falaq and An-Nās teach the believer to flee from created evil toward the Creator, while Al-Ikhlāṣ teaches the believer who the Creator is. The three surahs are therefore the complete nightly formula — know your Lord, then take refuge in Him from the external and internal harms of what He has made.

The surah’s central and most famous ḥadīth is the authentic Prophetic statement that it equals one-third of the Qur’an. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 7375 (with parallels in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 811, Jāmiʿ at-Tirmidhī 2900, Sunan Abī Dāwūd 1461) records Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī: a man heard his neighbor reciting Qul huwa Allāhu aḥad all night, nothing else, and asked the Prophet ﷺ about it. The Prophet ﷺ replied, “By the One in Whose hand is my soul, it equals one-third of the Qur’an.” The ḥadīth is in both Ṣaḥīḥs and the chain is beyond dispute. What the ḥadīth means, however, has been seriously misunderstood by lay readers across generations, and the classical mufassirūn insist on precision: equivalence here is in reward, not in textual substitution. Ibn Taymiyyah in Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā and Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī in Fatḥ al-Bārī (commentary on Bukhārī 7375) spell this out with unusual force: reciting Al-Ikhlāṣ three times earns the reward of reciting the whole Qur’an once, but it does not discharge the obligation to recite the Qur’an in ṣalāh, nor does it allow a Muslim to confine his learning to this surah alone. The reasoning Ibn Ḥajar gives is theological: the Qur’an is divided into three subject domains — commands and prohibitions (aḥkām), stories and parables (qaṣaṣ), and the names and attributes of Allah (asmāʾ wa ṣifāt) — and Al-Ikhlāṣ, in four verses, exhausts the third domain. It is the subject-matter third of the Qur’an condensed. The reward-equivalence follows from the content-equivalence, not the other way around.

The surah opens with Qul huwa Allāhu aḥad — “Say: He, Allah, is One.” Ibn Kathīr opens his commentary with the linguistic distinction between aḥad and wāḥid that lay readers almost always miss. Both words translate as “one” in English, but Arabic preserves a semantic range the English does not: wāḥid is numerical oneness — one in a sequence, which admits of a second — while aḥad is absolute oneness — unique, indivisible, admitting no second even as a possibility. Al-Qurṭubī in al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qur’an notes that aḥad in classical Arabic is used almost exclusively in negative constructions (mā jāʾanī aḥad — “no one came to me”); its deployment here as a positive affirmation of Allah is grammatically singular in the Qur’an and theologically decisive. The verse is not saying Allah is one of a kind; it is saying Allah is one in a way nothing else is one. The predicate huwa (“He”) before the subject Allāh is itself an emphasis in Arabic rhetoric — the pronoun of absolute pronominal reference identifies the One about to be defined before the Name is spoken. Ibn Kathīr draws the structural inference: the verse answers the pagan Quraysh and the Ahl al-Kitāb interlocutors who asked “describe your Lord to us” with a refusal to describe Him by analogy — the first self-definition Allah offers is a definition by exclusion of all parallel.

The second verse — Allāhu-ṣ-Ṣamad — contains the single most lexically rich attribute in the surah, and the classical mufassirūn record over twenty distinct linguistic readings of Ṣamad from the Ṣaḥābah and the Tābiʿūn. Ibn Kathīr in his tafsīr gathers them: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses Ṣamad as “the Master to whom all turn in need, who needs none”; Mujāhid as “the Enduring who neither eats nor drinks”; al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī as “the Everlasting after His creation perishes”; al-Shaʿbī as “the One free of all cavity and solid-through — nothing enters Him, nothing leaves Him”; al-Suddī as “the Sought-of, the Resorted-to”. Al-Qurṭubī organises the glosses into two centers of gravity: Ṣamad as the object of turning (al-maṣmūd ilayh — the One whom creation addresses in petition and gratitude) and Ṣamad as the Self-Sufficient Solid (al-dhī lā jawfa lahu — the One in whom there is no deficiency or interior to be filled). Both readings cohere: Allah is the One to whom all turn because He is the only being that needs no one. Ibn Taymiyyah in Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā argues the Qur’anic choice of Ṣamad as the second attribute — not al-Ḥayy, not al-ʿAlīm — is deliberate: after aḥad establishes that Allah is utterly unique, Ṣamad establishes why He is the only legitimate direction of worship — because every other being is deficient, needing, turning somewhere for its own sustenance.

The third and fourth verses — Lam yalid wa-lam yūlad • wa-lam yakun lahu kufuwan aḥad (“He neither begets nor is begotten • and there is none comparable to Him”) — complete the creed by negation. Ibn Kathīr identifies the three doctrines these verses refute: “He neither begets” rebuts the Christian ascription of sonship to Jesus, the Jewish ascription of sonship to ʿUzayr (per Al-Tawbah 9:30), and the pagan Quraysh ascription of daughters to Allah (banāt Allāh — the three idols al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā, Manāt, per Al-Najm 53:19–20). “Nor is begotten” rebuts every polytheistic cosmogony in which gods emerge from gods — the Greek, the Hindu, the Egyptian, the Mesopotamian, the pre-Islamic Arab — and establishes that Allah is uncaused. The final verse — and there is none comparable to Him — closes the creed with the broadest possible negation. Al-Qurṭubī notes that kufuwan covers equivalence in essence, in attribute, and in action; there is no being that shares Allah’s nature, no being that shares His attributes in the way He possesses them, and no being that acts with His independence. Ibn Taymiyyah frames the structure as a chiasm: verses one and four are negations of likeness (nothing like Him in oneness, nothing comparable to Him), verses two and three are affirmations of self-sufficiency and uncausedness. The surah is architecturally complete — a creed that cannot be shortened without breaking it, and cannot be extended without redundancy.

The authentic practice of the Prophet ﷺ with Al-Ikhlāṣ is as firm as its two Mu‘awwidhatān pair-mates. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5017 records the three-Quls nightly cupping-blowing-wiping sunnah. Sunan Abī Dāwūd 5082 and Jāmiʿ at-Tirmidhī 3575 (ḥasan per al-Albānī) record the three-times-after-Fajr-and-Maghrib practice from ʿAbdullāh ibn Khubayb. There is also a ḥadīth specific to Al-Ikhlāṣ that the classical commentators treat with special attention: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 7375 narrates the story of a Companion who led his tribe’s prayer in Madinah and recited Al-Ikhlāṣ in every rakʿah after the opening Fātiḥah, before adding whatever other surah he recited. His companions reported this to the Prophet ﷺ as if it were unusual; the Prophet ﷺ asked the man why. He said, “Because it is the description of al-Raḥmān and I love to recite it.” The Prophet ﷺ replied, “Tell him that Allah loves him.” Ibn Ḥajar in Fatḥ al-Bārī treats this narration as the fiqh ground for the permissibility — not just permissibility, but beloved status — of a worshipper tying himself devotionally to a particular passage of the Qur’an because of what it discloses about Allah. The surah is thus doubly weighted in the Prophet’s ﷺ practice: once as the content-third of the Qur’an whose reward-equivalence is in the Ṣaḥīḥayn, and again as the surah the Companions associated with the deepest love of the Divine Name.

The practical fiqh of Al-Ikhlāṣ follows this doctrinal weight. Recite it with the two Mu‘awwidhatān three times after Fajr and Maghrib and once after the other three prayers (ʿAbdullāh ibn Khubayb’s practice, Sunan Abī Dāwūd 5082). Recite the three before sleep with the Bukhārī 5017 blowing-and-wiping method. Recite it three times for the reward-equivalence of reciting the whole Qur’an once — but understand what this means and what it does not mean. It does not mean reciting it in place of the Qur’an in prayer; it does not mean a Muslim can confine himself to this surah; it does not mean the obligation to read the Qur’an regularly is lifted. It means — and the Ṣaḥīḥayn are explicit — that the three-times recitation earns the reward of a complete recitation. The honest grading matters: this is the only short surah with that specific wording in the Ṣaḥīḥayn, and the only short surah whose virtue is attributed by the Prophet ﷺ to the subject matter rather than the number of letters. Al-Ikhlāṣ is thus not a shortcut; it is a distillation — the entire doctrine of who Allah is compressed into four verses so that even a believer with limited memory or literacy carries the heart of the Qur’an within him.
